en: The Sūtra on the Bhikṣu of Campā Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakara of the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was staying at Campā, on the banks of the Gaṅgā, at the Dharma-lake.
On the water.
At that time, on the fifteenth day, the Blessed One sat before the community of bhikṣus to recite the precepts.
Once the Blessed One was seated, he observed the thoughts and intentions within the minds of the bhikṣus.
Having observed the thoughts in the minds of the bhikṣus, he sat in silence during the first watch of the night.
Then, a certain bhikṣu rose from his seat, adjusted his robes properly, joined his palms toward the Blessed One, and addressed the Blessed One, saying:
"Venerable Sir!..."
When one watch of the night had passed and the Blessed One and the community of bhikṣus had been seated for a long time, [the bhikṣu] said, "I pray that the Blessed One will recite the Prātimokṣa.
At that time, the Blessed One remained silent.
When the World-Honored One had sat in silence until midnight, that bhikṣu again joined his palms toward the World-Honored One and addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"The first watch of the night has passed; the middle watch of the night has passed, World-Honored One!
The community of bhikṣus has been seated for a long time; we only pray that the World-Honored One will recite the precepts."
At that time, the Blessed One also remained silent.
Then, after midnight had passed, the Blessed One sat in silence; the bhikṣu joined his palms toward the Blessed One and addressed him, saying:

“May the Blessed One know that the first watch of the night has passed, the middle watch has passed, and the latter half of the night has passed; the morning star is about to appear, and it will not be long before the morning star rises.”
“World-Honored One!
The community of bhikṣus has been seated for a long time; we only pray that the World-Honored One will recite the precepts.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed those bhikṣus, saying:
“There is one among my community of bhikṣus who is impure.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was also present in the assembly. Having joined the assembly, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana thought to himself:
“Which bhikṣu is the Blessed One speaking of?”
"I say that there is impurity among the assembly.
I should enter into a samādhi corresponding to that state, and with the mind of samādhi, observe the thoughts within the minds of the bhikṣus."

Thereupon, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana immediately entered a state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) just as it was described, and with a mind in *samādhi*, he observed the thoughts within the minds of the bhikṣus.
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana immediately knew that this was an act of the World-Honored One toward a bhikṣu.
Thereupon, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana arose from samādhi, went to where that bhikṣu was, and having arrived, took the bhikṣu by the arm and led him outside the door, saying:
"You fool, depart!"
"You should not stay here overnight; there is no bhikṣu who dwells with you, for you are now outside the community of bhikṣus.

Thereupon, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana took that bhikṣu by the arm, led him out the door, and closed it behind them. Having closed the door, he went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at the World-Honored One’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
Having stepped aside, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana addressed the Blessed One, saying:
“Blessed One!
Regarding those whom you call ‘monks,’ you have said there are impurities within the assembly; I have already taken that monk by the arm and led him outside the door.”
"You foolish man, depart! You should not stay here overnight; there is no bhikṣu who dwells together with you, for now the bhikṣus are outsiders to you.
"Indeed, World-Honored One!"

The first watch of the night has passed; midnight has passed; the period after midnight has passed; the night is about to dawn at the time when the morning star appears—the morning star is soon to rise.
“World-Honored One!
The community of bhikṣus has been seated for a long time; may the World-Honored One please recite the precepts.
“You, Maudgalyāyana!”
That foolish person has incurred great demerit by having provoked the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus. Maudgalyāyana,
if there were an impure bhikṣu within the assembly when the Tathāgata recited the precepts, that fool’s head would have split into seven pieces.
Therefore, Maudgalyāyana!
From this day forward, you all shall recite the precepts together; the Tathāgata will no longer come to recite them. Why is that?
Maudgalyāyana!

After this fool has passed through such [faults], he observes his movements—bending and stretching, withdrawing and extending—and while carrying his saṃghāṭī robe and bowl, he declares himself to be a practitioner of the holy life among other practitioners of the holy life.
"O Maudgalyāyana!
If someone says, 'This is a practitioner of the holy life,' yet another person thinks:
'The śramaṇa is an illusion; the śramaṇa is coarse; the śramaṇa is a thorn; the śramaṇa is not what he claims.'"
Having understood this, he then cast it outside. Why?
For fear of defiling other pure bhikṣus.

It is just as if, Maudgalyāyana, there were a field of rice or a field of barley that had been well-established, and within it some weeds grew; if the roots of those weeds were like the roots of the barley, and their stalks, joints, leaves, and fruit were likewise so, they should be discarded before they have produced seed.
"Maugandalyāyana!
Once the grain has been formed, that householder farmer then thinks:
'This is the weed that ruins the barley, the thorn of the barley, the blight of the barley.'"
He then pulled it out and cast it aside. Why was this?
For fear that it might spoil the remaining pure barley.
In this way, Maudgalyāyana!

If there is a foolish person who, having committed such transgressions, continues to observe them while bending and stretching, picking up and putting down his saṃghāṭī robe and alms bowl, yet declares himself a fellow practitioner of the holy life among other practitioners of the holy life.
If, Maudgalyāyana, someone who calls himself a practitioner of the holy life (brahmacarya) should think:
"This ascetic is corrupt; this ascetic is a thorn; this ascetic is coarse; this ascetic is not one who speaks [the truth]."
Having realized this, he then cast it outside.
Why? For fear that it might defile other pure bhikṣus.

It is just as, Maudgalyāyana, when a householder farmer in the winter months prepares a large grain stack; whatever of that grain remains firm and stable stays behind, while everything else—whether grass or leaves—is scattered into the wind and blown away entirely. That householder farmer holds a broom in his hand therein.
"Maugandalyāyana!
If a foolish person commits such an act of transgression, it is because he overlooks the grain [in his own hand].
It is even so, Maugandalyāyana!"

If a certain foolish person, having committed such transgressions of conduct, observes his own movements—bending and stretching, drawing in and extending—and while carrying his saṃghāṭī robe and bowl, claims among other practitioners of the holy life that he himself is a practitioner of the holy life.
If, Moggallāna, another who calls himself a practitioner of the holy life (brahmacārī) should think:
"This ascetic is ruined; this ascetic is coarse; this ascetic is a thorn."
Having realized this, he cast it away outside.
Why? For fear of causing harm to the other bhikṣus.
Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana!

That householder farmer, seeking water and wishing to channel it, took a very sharp axe and entered the forest. There he grasped his axe and struck at the trees, thinking that those trees which were firm and solid could not be penetrated.
That is to say, when a withered tree is struck, the axe sinks right in.
A householder cuts its roots; having cut the roots, he hollows out its interior; having hollowed out its interior, he constructs wooden conduits and channels to direct the water through it.
"So it is, Maudgalyāyana!
Suppose a certain foolish person,
having performed such an action, observes his own movements as he bends and stretches, contracts and expands."
Carrying the saṃghāṭī robe and the alms bowl, yet among other practitioners of the holy life (brahmacārin), he claims for himself the status of a practitioner of the holy life.
If, Maudgalyāyana!
He claims to be a practitioner of the holy life (*brahmacārin*), yet he thinks to himself:
"The śramaṇas are ruined; the śramaṇas are coarse; the śramaṇas are thorns; the śramaṇas are not [true] śramaṇas."
Having known this, he cast it away outside.
Why? For fear that he might cause harm to other pure bhikṣus.
He spoke in verse:
"Dwelling together and what one should know, Evil seeking and malice, Resentment, hatred,
and not abandoning greed, Not discarding illusion, flattery, and deceit."
The person from Zhāng lies about being at rest, claiming for himself that he is a śramaṇa;
yet he commits various evil deeds, and his evil views are not a source of joy.
He utters many false words; having recognized him as such, [one should avoid him].
They shall not associate with them at all, but shall banish them and not dwell together.
Knowing the proper time and possessing pure conduct, they distinguish who has finished their speech;
those who have not ceased from talk are not śramaṇas, and having been expelled for their evil deeds, they are cast out.
"Do not dwell with evil, whether repeatedly or day by day;
gather together [in virtue], and you shall reach the end of this suffering.
Thus spoke the Buddha, and having heard what the World-Honored One had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and were glad.
The Sutra on the Bhikṣu of Campā Spoken by the Buddha
